summary: Describes how to use the CMC certificate management protocol when managing certificates for the US government's NSA Suite B cryptography policy. It narrows the choices in RFC 5272, RFC 5273 and RFC 5274 to the algorithms that policy allows. It is informational, and its status is now historic.

eli5.summary: The government once published a short list of approved secret-code methods. This explains how to get computer ID cards using only methods on that list. It is now old and kept for history.

questions: how to manage suite b certificates
subtitle: How to manage certificates using Suite B cryptography.

tldr.problem: Organizations that need to use US government Suite B cryptography also need a standardized way to request, receive, and renew X.509 digital certificates that comply with Suite B algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC profiles the Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) protocol, a protocol for certificate enrollment and rekey, restricting all cryptographic operations to Suite B algorithms (ECDSA on P-256 or P-384, AES, and SHA-2).
tldr.outcome: Suite B is now Historic. The RFC serves as a reference for how to manage Suite B certificates within the constraints of the CMC protocol, useful for systems that must maintain Suite B compliance.

facts.label: Minimum secret strength
facts.value: 128 bits for P-256, 192 bits for P-384

today: RFC 6403 is Historic. It describes how to use CMC for managing Suite B certificates at a time when Suite B was an active government cryptography policy. The standards are maintained for systems that must support legacy Suite B configurations.

sections.title: Overview and Scope
sections.content:
This RFC specifies a profile of the Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) protocol for managing X.509 certificates that comply with Suite B cryptography. The CMC protocol, defined in RFCs 5272, 5273, and 5274, provides a framework for certificate enrollment (initial request), rekey (renewing a key pair with a new certificate), and certificate renewal. This profile restricts the CMC protocol to use only Suite B algorithms: ECDSA on the P-256 or P-384 elliptic curves paired with SHA-256 or SHA-384 hash functions, and AES for key wrapping when needed.

The profile covers interactions between three parties: a client (the entity requesting a certificate, such as a user or device), one or more Registration Authorities (RAs, which validate requests), and a Certification Authority (CA, which issues the certificates). The profile specifies the message formats, algorithm constraints, and procedural requirements for each party at every stage of the enrollment or rekey process.
sections.eli5: When you want a digital ID card from the government, you have to ask using their approved secret-code methods only, in a form they can understand.

sections.title: What Clients Must Do
sections.content:
When a client requests a certificate, it must use a Full PKI Request, which is an encrypted and signed message containing the actual certificate request. For a P-256 certificate request, the client may sign the Full PKI Request using either SHA-256 with ECDSA on P-256 or SHA-384 with ECDSA on P-384. For a P-384 request, the client must use SHA-384 with ECDSA on P-384.

The certificate request itself (either in PKCS#10 or CRMF format) must specify the key usage extensions according to Suite B rules and include a digital signature by the requested key as proof of possession. If the client does not yet have a signature certificate (such as during initial enrollment), it may sign the request using the private key for which the certificate is being requested, or with a key establishment key if applicable. For user authentication with SSH or other protocols, the client must include additional controls such as the Identity Proof Version 2 or POP Link Witness Version 2 when authenticating with a shared secret rather than an existing certificate.
sections.eli5: When you ask for your ID card, you have to sign your request using one of the government-approved secret-code methods, and prove that you have the secret key it mentions.

sections.title: What the Certification Authority Must Do
sections.content:
The Certification Authority receives requests from clients and RAs, validates them, and issues certificates. The CA must reject any request that uses non-Suite-B algorithms and return an error code. The CA must verify that any RA that signed the request is authorized to do so, checking the RA's certificate for appropriate Extended Key Usage values or CMS Content Constraints extensions.

When issuing a certificate in response to a client request, the CA must sign the response message using Suite B algorithms: either SHA-256 and ECDSA on P-256 or SHA-384 and ECDSA on P-384, depending on the request. If the response is to a P-384 request, or if the request contains both P-256 and P-384 certificate requests, the CA must use SHA-384 and ECDSA on P-384 to sign the response. The CA must use a separate certificate (not the certificate-signing key itself) to sign CMC responses, authorized through either an Extended Key Usage extension or CMS Content Constraints extension.
sections.eli5: The government ID office checks that your request is correctly signed and that anyone who helped you pass the check too. Then it signs your new ID card using the approved secret-code methods.

sections.title: Enrollment Scenarios and Shared Secrets
sections.content:
The RFC describes three ways a client can authenticate an initial enrollment request: with a previously installed signature certificate (such as one pre-installed by a manufacturer), with a shared secret distributed out-of-band, or through an RA. In the shared-secret scenario, the shared secret must provide at least 128 bits of cryptographic strength for P-256 requests and 192 bits for P-384 requests. The client uses the shared secret with a keyed hash algorithm (HMAC-SHA256 or HMAC-SHA384) to prove it knows the secret without revealing it.

For certificate rekey, the RFC distinguishes between rekey of a signature certificate (where the new key is used to authenticate the rekey request) and rekey of a key establishment certificate (where an existing signature certificate must authenticate the request). The RFC also specifies requirements for servers and CAs themselves when they need to obtain or renew their own Suite B certificates.
sections.eli5: You can prove you're allowed to get an ID card if you have an old one, if someone gave you a secret password, or if the government's office helped you prove it.
